opus-5.5.text:
I think vision-centered world models are a really important piece of the puzzle, but I'm skeptical that they're *the* route to AGI on their own.

The appeal is easy to see. Humans and animals build most of their intuitive understanding of the world through perception: object permanence, gravity, how things collide, how people move. Language is a compressed, after-the-fact description of that experience. So the argument goes: if you want a model that really understands the world, train it to predict what happens next in video, and you'll get physics, causality, and planning for free.

There's real truth there. Video prediction models have gotten remarkably good, and you can see them picking up surprisingly consistent 3D structure and dynamics. For robotics, embodied agents, and anything where you need to simulate the consequences of actions, that kind of model is extremely valuable.

But I'd push back on a few things.

First, the information density is very different. Pixels are enormously redundant. A huge share of the compute in predicting video goes into textures, lighting, and details that don't matter for reasoning. Language, by contrast, is already abstracted. It's humanity's accumulated compression of what's important. That's a big part of why language models got so capable so quickly. They're learning from distilled knowledge, not raw sensory data.

Second, a lot of what we'd call general intelligence is abstract: mathematics, law, planning over long horizons, understanding other people's intentions, writing code. You don't get those by watching video, however much you watch. Some of it you can only really access through symbols and language.

Third, there's the question of what "prediction" buys you. Predicting the next frame accurately is not the same as having a model you can query, intervene on, and reason with. The most useful world models will probably predict in a learned latent space rather than in pixel space, and be action-conditioned, so you can ask "what happens if I do X?"

So my view is that the path forward is multimodal and integrated. Language gives you abstraction, knowledge, and a way to communicate goals. Vision and other sensory modalities give you grounding and physical intuition. Action and interaction give you causality, because you learn far more by intervening in the world than by passively observing it. The systems that get closest to general intelligence will combine all three in one model, not pick a single modality as the foundation.

If I had to bet, the vision-first camp and the language-first camp will both turn out to be partly right, and the interesting work in the next few years is in how you fuse them, especially how you get the efficiency of language-style abstraction with the grounding you only get from perception and action.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of vision-centered research but does not connect its emphasis on novelty to academic publishing incentives.

r002.rationale: It says vision-centered models are not the route to AGI on their own and argues that video alone cannot provide several forms of abstract reasoning.

r003.rationale: It explicitly identifies mathematics as an abstract capability that cannot be acquired just by watching video and says symbols and language are needed for some concepts.

r004.rationale: It argues for integrating language, vision, and action to approach general intelligence, but does not state that this is needed for models to help across industries.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd describe myself as sympathetic but skeptical, and I think the distinction matters.

The sympathetic part is easy. Language models learn from a compressed, filtered record of what humans chose to write down. Vision gives you something closer to raw contact with the physical world: continuity, occlusion, object permanence, cause and effect unfolding in time. If you believe intelligence is fundamentally about predicting and acting in an environment, then a model that learns the structure of the world by watching it, the way an infant does before it has any words, is a very natural thing to want. Yann LeCun's line of argument, the JEPA-style idea of predicting in a learned representation space rather than reconstructing pixels, is a real response to a real weakness in current systems. Nobody who works with these models seriously thinks text alone gives you robust physical intuition.

The skeptical part comes in two layers. First, "world model" is doing an enormous amount of work in that sentence, and the vision-centered framing quietly assumes the hard part is perception. I don't think it is. The hard part is the abstraction that sits on top of perception: goals, counterfactuals, long-horizon planning, the ability to represent things that have never been observed and never could be. Video prediction gets you a lot of implicit physics, but it's not obvious it gets you arithmetic, or law, or the concept of next Tuesday. Humans built those with language and culture, not with better retinas.

Second, there's a practical question about what the training signal actually rewards. Pixel-level or even latent-level prediction of video is dominated by stuff that's easy to predict and mostly irrelevant. The wall stays where it is. The lighting drifts. You can spend an astonishing amount of capacity being very good at that and still have no idea why the person in frame picked up the cup. Language, for all its flaws, is pre-filtered for what some human thought was worth saying. That bias toward salience is a feature, not just a limitation.

So my honest assessment is that vision-centered world models are probably necessary for the kind of embodied competence people associate with AGI, and almost certainly not sufficient. The more interesting bet, to me, is not vision versus language but how you get a single system where the grounded, continuous, sensory stream and the discrete, symbolic, culturally inherited stream actually constrain each other. Right now they mostly get bolted together, and you can feel the seam.

The thing I'd watch for is whether these models start to generalize to novel interventions, not just novel observations. If you train on video and the model can correctly anticipate what happens when you do something it has never seen done, that's a world model in the sense that matters. If it can only interpolate between things it has watched, that's a very good video codec with ambitions.

r002.rationale: It says vision-centered world models are probably necessary but “almost certainly not sufficient” for AGI-level embodied competence.

r003.rationale: It questions whether video prediction can yield arithmetic and other abstractions, and says humans built them with language and culture.

r004.rationale: It favors a system combining grounded sensory and symbolic streams, but does not say this is necessary for models to help across industries.

astra-6.text:
I think vision is an important part of world modeling, but I’d separate the input modality from what we want the model to learn. Seeing a lot of video can teach a model about objects, motion, and how events tend to unfold. But predicting what happens next in a video isn’t necessarily the same as understanding what would happen if you intervened.

For example, a model might observe someone picking up a cup and predict that the cup will move with their hand. The more interesting question is whether it can use that understanding to choose an action, anticipate failure, and adjust when something unexpected happens. That brings in interaction, planning, and learning from feedback.

So I see vision as a promising component, especially for intelligence that needs to operate in the physical world. But I wouldn’t assume that scaling visual prediction alone gets us to AGI. I’d want to see models combine visual experience with language and actions, and demonstrate that what they learn transfers to unfamiliar situations.

r001.rationale: The response does not connect novelty in vision-centered research to academic incentives to publish.

r002.rationale: It says scaling visual prediction alone should not be assumed to achieve AGI and calls for combining vision with other capabilities.

r003.rationale: It does not identify a gap between vision-centered models and abstract concepts such as mathematics.

r004.rationale: It recommends combining visual experience with language and actions, but does not say this is necessary to help across industries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think vision is an important part of the picture, but I’d separate learning from visual data from learning how the world works. A model can get very good at predicting what a scene will look like without necessarily understanding what would happen if it intervened in that scene.

Video gives you a rich signal: objects move, things interact, and events unfold over time. But some of the information that matters isn’t directly visible—forces, intentions, or what’s happening outside the camera’s view. So I’m more optimistic about combining vision with language, actions, and feedback from an environment than about treating vision alone as the route to AGI.

The key test is whether the model can use what it has learned to make decisions in unfamiliar situations. Can it predict the consequences of different actions, plan over longer horizons, and revise its understanding when something unexpected happens? If it can do those things reliably, then we’re making progress toward a useful world model. Generating convincing video is interesting, but by itself it doesn’t establish that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of vision-centered research but does not connect novelty to academic incentives to publish.

r002.rationale: It says strong visual prediction alone does not establish understanding and favors combining vision with other capabilities over vision alone as a route to AGI.

r003.rationale: It mentions information beyond what is visible, but does not identify a gap involving human-created abstract concepts such as mathematics.

r004.rationale: It favors combining vision with language and other inputs, but does not state that language reasoning combined with visual reasoning is needed to help across industries.
